item.title: The UK has finally nailed the vocabulary of orbital warfare. Now it needs a playbook.
item.description: The past year has changed how the British government talks about space. The Strategic Defence Review put space on par with land, sea and air as a warfighting domain. The Defence Investment Plan earmarked more than 3 billion pounds ($4 billion) for space over four years and named offensive and defensive space control without flinching. The UK Space Strategy, published in September, put defense and national security first. And at the UK Space Power Conference the Defence Secretary announced No. 3 Space Effects Squadron, the country’s first unit dedicated to the Control of Space mission, and spoke plainly about orbital warfare and counter-satellite weapons. After years in which the sector could barely say these things aloud, they are now being said clearly from the top.

item.title: Turning capacity into capability: recommendations for America’s ground station infrastructure.
item.description: The commercial space industry is rapidly adding ground station capacity around the world. This collective investment will lower the cost of antenna access, increase supply and lower prices — but counterintuitively, more antenna capacity does not necessarily translate to capability across the diverse landscape of satellite operators and missions.
